title: Monopoly Round-Up: AI Cockroaches Scurry Out from Under Nvidia, the Most Valuable Company in the World
author: Matt Stoller
content:
Lots of news, as usual. AI continues to dominate much of the political
discourse, in part because spending on things like data centers has exploded
while spending on everything else we need, from housing to education to
manufacturing, has declined. Meanwhile, the Pope continues to deliver hot
takes, reminding us there are hugely significant moral questions underlying
the political and economic debates:

Before we get to the Good and the Bad news, after the jump for paid
subscribers only, I want to highlight an important but little-noticed story
that has implications for the AI bubble, and particularly, for the most
valuable company in the world, Nvidia. Nvidia is the center of the AI
revolution, with its software layer CUDA and its AI chips dominating training
and inference for models. It is worth $6 trillion, and its CEO, Jensen Huang,
is now a global superstar who regularly sits down with national leaders and
puts Donald Trump on [speakerphone](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/donald-
trump/nvidia-ceo-jensen-huang-ai-speakerphone-all-hands-meeting-rcna597761) at
major conferences.

Nvidia, despite its immense profits and prestige, is known for doing something
a bit scuzzy, called "circular financing." That is, it invests in its own
customers so they can buy its chips. Sometimes it goes through multiple
layers, like investing in OpenAI, which buys from Oracle, which buys from
Nvidia. But there are a host of smaller AI companies in which Nvidia, as well
as hedge funds and banks, have put a lot of money. And one of them, a little
noticed AI data center company called Firmus, tried to sell shares to on the
stock market this week. Yet investors revolted, and the company
[had](https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/australian-nvidia-backed-ai-
data-centre-operator-firmus-shelves-ipo-2026-10-08/) to scrap its initial
public offering.

Aside from Nvidia, Firmus was backed by blue chip financial firms Jane Street
and Blackstone, and it was set to become Australia's biggest IPO ever, at $30
billion in valuation. So this failure is a big deal, and it raised eyebrows
all over Wall Street.

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!tSps!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fea47253e-f545-4b0d-a3bc-c50a9aed41db_803x230.png)

What happened? It turns out, Firmus executives got a little too greedy. In a
normal initial public offering, companies restrict insiders from selling their
shares for a time period. There are a few reasons to do so. First, restricting
insiders sales is a vote of confidence in the new firm, a statement from
executives and early investors that "hey yeah we want your money investors,
but we have skin in the game in the form of owning our own stock." Second,
it's a statement that the stock won't be met with a lot of immediate selling
pressure in the markets, since insiders can't dump their shares.

This time, however, Firmus [set up
terms](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-06/firmus-stock-
overhang-said-to-make-some-investors-wary-on-ipo) to let them sell
immediately, meaning those who were most in-the-know wanted to cash out ASAP.
That looks bad, a clear indication that insiders don't think the company is a
valuable going concern but see it as a temporary vehicle for self-enrichment.
On a practical level, huge selling pressure would have flooded the market and
crushed investors. So money managers, after being harmed with Paramount bonds,
SpaceX, and a number of others, refused to bid, and the banks behind Firmus
had to pull the offering. It's one of the biggest flops in recent capital
markets history.

What matters here are three things. First, the Firmus IPO was backed by the
most prestigious companies in AI. Second, there are many companies like
Firmus. And third, the company's
co-[founder](https://www.news.com.au/finance/money/wealth/jailed-
aussies-6-billion-redemption/news-story/a5d4103de9729b60ba6ec60ff2b0d914),
Oliver Curtis, has a criminal background in stock manipulation, and yet the
banks still went ahead with the offering. Yes, you read that right:

> A decade ago, Oliver Curtis was at the lowest point in his life as he was
> sent to prison for pocketing $1.4 million in insider trading. Now, he is one
> of the richest people in Australia and preparing for a $6 billion move he
> sees as his redemption.

There's another co-founder of Firmus, Tim Rosenfeld. He's not a criminal, but
he's a cousin of Curtis, and his
[background](https://archive.is/20260421195149/https:/www.afr.com/rear-
window/the-other-firmus-co-founder-20260421-p5zpsd) was running a loss-making
lingerie company called Steadmark.

What makes this situation more than a run of the mill scam is the involvement
of Nvidia in Firmus and its criminal co-founder. Why would Nvidia get in bed
with a crook? Well, Firmus is in an important industry segment that generates
demand for Nvidia chips. Firmus is a "neocloud," which are basically racks of
servers funded by venture capitalists and Nvidia to buy chips and rent out
computing power. Think of a neocloud as a way to keep debt off the books of
the big AI firms. Neoclouds are a corporate shell containing real estate,
chips, and financing. Often there are multiple layers of investors, phantom
contracts or insider self-dealing, all wrapped in a narrative that they are
engaged in "advanced AI" deployment.

This move has tended to work because of the involvement of the most
prestigious players in AI. When Nvidia (or Google or Anthropic) backstops or
does business with a neocloud, investors think there must be something there.
So the neocloud's valuation goes up a lot. Then that neocloud raises more
money at a high valuation, announces more data centers, and orders more chips.
That's more profits for Nvidia, more investments, and so on and so forth.

These investments take place in the private market, with hedge funds and
insiders thinking they are getting in at a low valuation. They often don't
even care if there's a good business model here, since they think someone else
will be left holding the bag. The business model never really made much sense,
with Firmus starting as a bitcoin miner, before pivoting to AI. But it didn't
matter, because Firmus was about to sell shares to the last set of investors
out there - you and me in the public markets. Fortunately, it looks like the
public market participants have wisened up, at least in this case.

Firmus, however, is not the only scam in the AI space. Many such neoclouds
started as bitcoin miners before jumping to the AI boom, often funded by a
prestigious AI firm like Nvidia. And that suggests there's something systemic
going on.

Here are a few other neocloud or adjacent plays: There's TeraWulf, which has
big leasing deals with [Anthropic](https://investors.terawulf.com/news-
events/press-releases/detail/142/terawulf-announces-anthropic-lease-at-
justified-data-campus-and-sale-of-majority-interest-in-abernathy-joint-
venture-to-fluidstack) and [Google](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/google-
backs-terawulf-shift-bitcoin-031835960.html), and whose backers have been
allegedly caught engaged in market manipulation. Google bankrolled the
company's shift from bitcoin mining to AI data center. Here's [Grizzly
Research](https://grizzlyreports.com/beware-of-terawulf-we-believe-the-
company-is-a-charade-to-enrich-insiders-at-the-cost-of-investors-and-backed-
by-notorious-pump-and-dump-artists/):

> Our research uncovers that TeraWulf's third-largest shareholder is an entity
> controlled by the wife of John O'Rourke, the disgraced CEO of Riot
> Blockchain, who was charged for his part of a $27 million "Lucrative Market
> Manipulation Schemes" by the SEC.

There's Sharon AI, a [competitor to
Firmus](https://archive.is/20260219021404/https:/www.afr.com/technology/firmus-
rival-sharon-ai-debuts-with-1b-valuation-on-nasdaq-20260219-p5o3k5), which
also [has deals](https://sharonai.com/press-releases/sharon-ai-announces-six-
year-strategic-compute-collaboration-with-nvidia/) with Nvidia and is backed
by Oaktree Capital management. Here's [Sharon AI's
owner](https://www.afr.com/rear-window/sharon-ai-s-founder-is-burning-down-
the-house-20260505-p5ztu5), who was involved in a mysterious fire:

> James Manning's colourful past involves owning Sydney's historic White Bay
> hotel. He was interviewed by police after the site burnt down in 2008.
> Manning isn't a familiar face, and not running a multibillion-dollar ASX-
> listed company. But his AI "neocloud" operator listed on the Nasdaq earlier
> this year.

There's Applied Digital. According to [the Bear
Cave](https://www.fieldsonginvestments.com/blog/are-nvidia-and-applied-
digital-manipulating-their-financials), this company started by providing
staff to production companies, pivoted to plasma technology, then processing
potatoes, then to blockchain, and finally to AI with [financing from
Nvidia](https://ir.applieddigital.com/news-events/press-
releases/detail/107/applied-digital-announces-160-million-strategic-financing)
in 2024. However, here it gets creepier, since Nvidia
[sold](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/nvidia-just-sold-stake-
applied-204000170.html) its stake in 2026, after Applied Digital had bought
its chips with billions in borrowed money.

There are so many of these dodgy firms with no obvious business model and
billions or tens of billions of valuation. Nscale. Celsius Mining. Coreweave.
Nebius. Crusoe. SB Energy. Hut 8. Lancium. Iren. Bitdeer. And so on and so
forth. With lots of stories like
[this](https://www.thetimes.com/business/companies-markets/article/josh-payne-
was-a-builder-how-did-he-become-a-billionaire-in-two-years-t0m0bmtn8).

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!uKLi!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F01ca4eae-defa-4dfd-
bd96-73081368a7fe_692x318.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!uKLi!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F01ca4eae-defa-4dfd-
bd96-73081368a7fe_692x318.png)

How did I hear of this situation? Well there's a document floating around Wall
Street that describes this set of companies. Short-sellers, and there aren't
that many left, know the best way to understand where the scammers are isn't
to look at a particular industry sector, but to follow the scammers from
industry to industry. As a contact put it, "This is like the SPAC craze of
2021. Whatever the hot thing of the day is, that is what the grifters will
gravitate to. Shell companies did reverse takeovers with Chinese firms, the
biotech bubble, shale, and others. Stock promoters will promote." In other
words, the same people just move from scam to scam, since unethical stock
promotion itself is their business.

This whole scene is reminiscent of a specific part of the global financial
crisis in 2008, which had a similar dynamic. Subprime lenders like Ameriquest
were fly-by-night operations that somehow suddenly grew into multi-billion
dollar lenders from 2003 onward. These guys weren't particularly good at
credit analysis, they were simply promoters willing to break the law. As Joe
Nocera and Bethany McLean wrote in _All the Devils Are Here,_ some salesmen
were using meth or cocaine to lend more money to bad credit risks.

Now, at some level, this situation made no sense. Lending out money that was
sure not to be paid back is a bad business. However, there is one way in which
losing money deliberately can be quite profitable. If you are charging fees on
your loans, and the money you are losing is not yours, then it works out
great, at least for the scammer. But how did these operators get access to
huge amounts of capital?

Here's where the analogy to Nvidia comes in. The actual prestigious actors
losing other people's money were companies like Goldman Sachs, Deutsche Bank,
Morgan Stanley, and so forth, who were backstopping these subprime lenders
with warehouse lines of credit. This loan was a special kind of facility that
let the subprime lenders keep lending, and then send the mortgages they were
creating to Wall Street, where they would be processed into mortgage-backed
securities.

These securities were then sold to pension funds, who bore losses. Sometimes,
as Naked Capitalism [noted](https://www.nakedcapitalism.com/2009/12/body-
count-from-goldman-actions-crosses-into-criminal-territory.html), Goldman was
even shorting these securities, so they _wanted_ bad credit risks. At any
rate, the prestige of Wall Street banks masked the obvious graft going on, and
the credit tripwires that ordinarily would have slowed a credit cycle. Michael
Lewis wrote up a fake version of this story in _The Big Short,_ portraying
Wall Street bankers as foolish instead of on the take.

Since we never fixed anything in our credit markets, we keep having such
scams, whether the fracking guys, the China reverse mergers, WeWork, crypto
and Sam Bankman-Fried, and now, the AI neoclouds. But the scamming isn't just
a result of grifters who want to steal, those kinds of people are always
around. It's that Nvidia, with its immense prestige on Wall Street and access
to power in DC, is playing the role of Goldman in 2005. And with the important
exception of Elizabeth Warren, there's not a lot of interest in reimposing any
controls on capital.

That's not good. It's also not surprising.

All that said, the residual memory of scams and crises and bailouts among the
public is real, and impossible to ignore. And in a few weeks, voters may
decide they'd like to have Elizabeth Warren holding the gavel running the
Senate Banking Committee.

And now, the rest of the monopoly news round-up. Lots of interesting updates,
including a major new lawsuit against hotel booking site Expedia, and more
handouts for airlines from by 90's Real World cast member and current
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy. Read on for more after the flip.

cockroaches)
